A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned. She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation. She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy.

On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.” A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area. There were no signs of steroid-induced atrophy, such as skin thinning or increased vascular prominence.

A 14-year-old girl presented with a 6-year history of a photosensitive eruption involving her face, neck, trunk, and extremities. Her symptoms began at age 8 years. She had previously tried multiple medications including systemic steroids, hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, tofacitinib, rituximab, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), with minimal improvement.

Clinical examination revealed:- Violaceous erythema on forehead and midface- Diffuse poikiloderma involving upper chest, anterolateral thighs, and extensor arms- Erythematous, flat-topped papules on extensor joints of hands- Nailfold examination showed dilated capillary loops, capillary dropout, and ragged cuticles

clinical_record:
An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

A 56-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of polyarthralgia over the bilateral wrists, knees, ankles, and left shoulder, associated with early morning stiffness and swelling of the affected joints. Once-daily celecoxib provided significant but incomplete pain relief. He noted diffuse swelling over both feet and ankles and mild puffiness of his left hand. He had no rashes, nail changes, uveitis, or constitutional symptoms. He had a 6-month duration of cough associated with occasional blood streaks, with no previous smoking history.

Synovitis was elicited over both ankles. Bilateral lower limb pitting edema up to the ankles was noted. Reduced breath sounds were heard over the right upper zone. There was no clubbing or cervical lymphadenopathy.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 40.0 mm/h
  - C-reactive protein: 41.0 mg/L
  - Rheumatoid factor: negative
  - Serum creatinine: 73.0 µmol/L (0.83 mg/dL)
  - Serum albumin: 37.0 g/L (within normal range)

- Imaging Studies:
  - Radiographs of hands, knees, ankles, and left shoulder: unremarkable for erosions
  - Chest radiograph: 8.1×6.4-cm mass in the right upper zone
  - Computed tomography of chest: lesion with paratracheal lymphadenopathy

  - Endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of mediastinal lymph nodes: ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma with mucinous features

clinical_record:
A 12-month-old Caucasian boy presented with convulsive seizures lasting 3-4 seconds, characterized by faltering, smirking with withdrawal of the head and eyes. At birth, the patient had a blond hair strand, polydactyly of the right hand, and cardiac rhabdomyoma. At four months, depigmented spots appeared on the torso. First convulsive seizures noted at 8 months. Psychomotor development was normal for age. No family history of similar conditions.

No focal neurological symptoms were observed during examinations. Physical features included:- Blond hair strand- Polydactyly of right hand- Depigmented spots on torso

- Imaging Studies:  * Brain CT scan showed:    - Massive neoplasm formation in posterior cranial fossa    - Tubers    - Triventricular hydrocephalus    - Arachnoid cyst of left temporal region      * Brain MRI with contrast revealed:    - Extracranial solid mass in posterior fossa with brain stem compression    - Subcortical tubers in white matter of frontal lobes    - Triventricular hydrocephalus    - Arachnoid cyst of left temporal region      - Genetic Testing:    * Blood sample revealed TSC1 gene mutation (15 exon c.1690 G > T, p.E564*)      - Histopathology:    * Solid lobulated growth pattern    * Large epithelioid cells with clear/eosinophilic cytoplasm    * Moderate to severe cytologic atypia    * 35 mitotic events per high-power field    * Ki67 proliferation index around 15%    * Positive immunostaining for EMA, S100, Pan-Cytokeratin, and Brachyury

What is the most likely diagnosis?
reference_diagnosis: Clivus chordoma associated with Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC)
